findings.title: Paywall regression turns long-time users into detractors, but subscription value is still polarizing
findings.summary: Many long-time users report that workouts and features that used to be free now require a subscription, often after an update or reinstall. They describe feeling locked out and betrayed, calling the app 'money hungry' or a 'bait-and-switch'. However, a smaller set of subscribers says the subscription is worth the cost, cheaper than a gym, and delivers real results. The same monetization shift therefore creates a sharp split in perceived value.

findings.title: Trial, billing, and account failures break trust in the subscription
findings.summary: A substantial cluster of reviews reports being charged immediately after signing up for a free trial, being charged after cancellation, being unable to cancel, and having trouble with account login, data syncing, or unresponsive support. Users describe these as scams or trust-breaking experiences. These issues directly undermine the subscription model and can cause even paying users to stop using the app.

findings.title: Aggressive ads and in-app redirects disrupt the core workout experience
findings.summary: Free users report 90-second or longer ads before almost every workout, with some ads impossible to close, looping back into another ad, or failing to return to the workout. In several cases, the app redirects to the Shein website mid-session. These interruptions break the workout flow and are a major driver of churn among free users, though a few users accept ads as a fair trade for free access.

findings.title: Workout content is polarizing: praised for short, effective, varied sessions, criticized for repetition and AI-generated demos
findings.summary: Many reviewers love the core workout experience: short 30–45 second exercises, wide variety, clear demonstrations, and noticeable results (weight loss, soreness, habit building). Others, including long-time users, say newer workouts are repetitive, feel like 'AI slop', that exercise names and animations sometimes mismatch, and that pre-natal or specialized programs contain unsafe moves. The same workout library draws both 5-star praise and strong criticism, making it the clearest polarizing feature.

findings.title: Personalization and constraint settings are ignored, frustrating users with specific needs
findings.summary: Users who specify body areas to avoid, complete the intro quiz, or select no-jumping or pregnancy-safe settings report that the app still serves exercises that violate those constraints. Examples include 'legs every day and no arms' despite avoidance, squats/lunges when 'avoid knees' is set, and prenatal workouts that include lying-on-stomach moves. A single premium user could not find any way to turn off jumping. These failures break trust in the app's customization promises.

findings.title: AI-generated body imagery and weight-loss-first framing alienate wellness-focused users
findings.summary: A small but vocal set of users criticizes the app's use of AI-generated, hyper-sexualized body imagery instead of real diverse bodies, and an onboarding that forces a weight-loss goal and attaches weight-loss notes to every exercise. One reviewer calls the anti-fat framing 'vile' and harmful for people with eating-disorder histories. These complaints suggest the app's visual identity and messaging conflict with an inclusive, wellness-oriented brand.

findings.title: Users request granular workout controls and specialized routines
findings.summary: Reviewers who otherwise like the app ask for concrete improvements: an option to count reps instead of timers, less wordy/less distracting sound cues, Apple Watch calorie integration, pregnancy-safe strength/mobility workouts, and programs for older users with stiff joints. These are actionable opportunities to improve the core workout experience.
